Sources and how they are rated

Each article page lists the sources the article cites, who added each citation, and how several raters rate those sources. No rater is treated as the truth, and this project adds no rating of its own.

The raters

In short: The outside organisations whose ratings we show, what each one measures, and where its data comes from.

  • Wikipedia's own rating. The Perennial sources list, where Wikipedia editors record their consensus on sources they discuss often: generally reliable, no consensus, generally unreliable, deprecated or blacklisted. About 530 entries. Some people argue that these ratings lean in one political direction, which is one reason the independent assessments are shown beside them. Snapshot of 9 list pages taken 2026-11-11.
  • Independent quality score. Lin, H., Lasser, J., Lewandowsky, S., Cole, R., Gully, A., Rand, D. G. & Pennycook, G. (2023). High level of correspondence across different news domain quality rating sets. PNAS Nexus 2(9), pgad286. https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgad286 It combines six independent rating sets from fact-checkers, journalists and researchers into one score per news website, from 0 (lowest quality) to 1 (highest). Wikipedia is not one of the six. 11,520 websites.
  • Audience leaning. Robertson, R. E., Jiang, S., Joseph, K., Friedland, L., Lazer, D. & Wilson, C. (2018). Auditing partisan audience bias within Google Search. Proc. ACM Hum.-Comput. Interact. 2(CSCW), 148. https://doi.org/10.1145/3274417 For each website, whether its links were shared more by registered Democrats (towards −1) or Republicans (towards +1) among about 500,000 US voters on Twitter in 2017. It describes who shared a site, not what the site publishes. 19,022 websites.
  • AllSides (2018). AllSides Media Bias Ratings (2018 values as included in the Robertson et al. release), AllSides.com, licensed CC BY-NC 4.0. Left, lean left, centre, lean right or right, for a few hundred outlets.
  • Media Bias/Fact Check (MBFC). Media Bias/Fact Check ratings (bias and factual reporting), as collected in the Idiap Research Institute's open dataset (Factual-Reporting-and-Political-Bias-Web-Interactions, Apache-2.0). A political bias label (left to right, or least biased) and a factual-reporting label for about 4,400 news outlets, many outside the United States. MBFC is also one of the six rating sets in the independent quality score. Wikipedia's own list rates Media Bias/Fact Check as generally unreliable.
  • Academic level. Publication Forum (JUFO), Federation of Finnish Learned Societies: levels 0 to 3 assigned by panels of researchers to academic publishers, journals and series. Level 1 means the panels judge a publisher or journal to meet the basic criteria of academic publishing; 2 and 3 are the higher levels; 0 means it was assessed and does not meet them. The Danish register's level is shown where the record gives it. Only publishers and journals the register lists can have a level.
  • Kind of source and recorded associations. From Wikidata: what kind of body a source is (newspaper, academic publisher, think tank, advocacy group, court and so on, from the classes Wikidata assigns), and links recorded there: founded by, parent organisation, member of, affiliation, funded by, sponsor, chair, publisher, indexed in, and designation as a terrorist organisation by a government or international body. Each is a statement on Wikidata, linked so it can be checked. A link records a connection; it is not a rating.
  • Wikidata. Facts entered by volunteers on Wikidata, Wikipedia's sister database: country, current owner, political alignment and ideology where recorded, and whether it is classed as state media, a public broadcaster or a state-owned enterprise. Retrieved 2026-11-11.
Read with care: Wikipedia's own list (Perennial sources) rates about 530 sources that its editors argue about often. Most sources are not on it; that is not a bad mark. The quality score (Lin and colleagues, 2023) runs from 0 to 1 and covers news websites. Books and journals have no score. Audience leaning says who shares a website, not what it publishes: −1 means only Democrats shared it, +1 only Republicans, 0 both equally. Out of every 100 people sharing it, Republicans = (1 + score) ÷ 2 × 100, so −0.4 is about 70 Democrats to 30 Republicans. It comes from US Twitter users matched to voter records (DomainDemo, 2025; Robertson and colleagues, 2018) and covers only websites shared widely enough. Few publishers have a recorded political affiliation, and those records are written by volunteers on Wikidata and Wikipedia. The ratings are today's ratings, not the ratings when the footnote was added. Links between organisations (owner, founder, member of) come from Wikidata, which anyone can edit. † marks a fact for which Wikidata gives no source.

Wikipedia's ratings next to independent ratings

In short: For sources on Wikipedia's own reliability list, Wikipedia's rating side by side with the outside raters' scores.

All 534 entries on Wikipedia's list, cited in the analysed articles or not, with the independent scores for their websites where those exist. Each entry counts once. Entries without a website (for example, books) have no independent score.

Most-cited sources, by topic area

In short: The sources cited most often in each topic, with every rating we have for each.

Each table lists the 50 sources cited most often in that area's analysed articles. An article in several areas is counted under the area it is shown under.

How the summary rows are calculated. For the sources in scope that have a score s (independent quality, 0 to 1; or audience leaning, −1 to +1), each cited c times: mean per source = (s1 + … + sn) ÷ n, each source counted once; mean per citation = (c1·s1 + … + cn·sn) ÷ (c1 + … + cn), each source counted as often as it is cited. Both cover only scored sources: the share of citations they cover is given beside them. The rows cover every citation in scope, not only the sources listed in the table.

Organisations cited: checklist and recorded associations

In short: Think tanks, campaign groups, charities and other organisations that are cited, with public facts about each: official registration, funders, founders and links to other organisations.

The same checklist is applied to every organisation listed: registration in a public registry (with a link to the official record), recorded funders, founders, leadership, affiliations, political alignment, any terrorist designation, ratings by Wikipedia and by independent raters, a Wikipedia article, and for US non-profits the latest public tax filing. Each item is either found, with its evidence, or not found in these records, which is not the same as absent. There is no total and no score.

Think tanks, advocacy and activist groups, human rights organisations, charities and foundations, NGOs, religious organisations, trade unions, political parties and armed organisations cited in the analysed articles, and any organisation a government or international body has designated as terrorist. Each association is a statement on Wikidata, linked so it can be checked; organisations with none recorded show a dash. † marks a statement for which Wikidata cites no source (anyone can edit Wikidata). A recorded connection is not a rating, and an organisation without one may simply not have it entered on Wikidata.

Opinion and harder-to-check citations: the sources behind them

In short: Which sources the harder-to-check footnotes (opinion pieces, no link, paywall, no translation) point to.

Citations to opinion, comment or blog sections, and citations a reader would find harder to check, with how far their sources are profiled. Identified: the citation names or links a source. Rated: at least one rater on this page rates the source. Kind known: Wikidata records what kind of body it is. Anything recorded: rated, kind known, or found on Wikidata at all. Books: publishers, where their ISBNs were issued, and languages

In short: The books cited, grouped by the country or language area that issued their ISBN, with their languages and publishers.

21,247 different books are cited by ISBN in the analysed articles (27,858 citations). Open Library has a record of 18,143 (85%). Where a citation names no publisher, the publisher was taken from Open Library's record of the ISBN for 1,005 citations, and from the Wikidata item that holds the ISBN's publisher prefix for 38; 1,837 book citations still name no publisher. 6 cited ISBNs fail their check digit.

An ISBN is issued by a national or language-area agency, and its first digits say which (the International ISBN Agency's range file). That is where the publisher registered, not necessarily the language of the book. Languages are as Open Library records them.

Publishers of books not in English or registered outside the English-language ISBN groups

In short: Publishers of cited books that are not in English, or were registered outside English-speaking countries, with what is known about each.

A book is listed when its citation gives a language other than English, Open Library records it only in other languages, or its ISBN was issued by an agency other than the English-language groups (978-0, 978-1, and 979-8 for the United States). For each publisher, the same checklist: found on Wikidata, classed there as a self-publishing company, owner or parent organisation, founders, affiliations, political alignment, an academic level from the Finnish register, Wikipedia articles in any language, and ratings. Each item is found, with its evidence, or not found in these records, which is not the same as absent. There is no score. † marks a Wikidata statement with no source given there.

What cited websites say about themselves

In short: What each cited website's own pages say about who runs it: company names, registration numbers, copyright owners and tracking accounts.

9,913 cited websites that no rater rates, or that Wikidata classes as an organisation, were read by fixed rules: the home page and up to three of the site's own pages that usually name the body behind it (about, legal notice, privacy policy). Where the site refused or could not be reached, the Internet Archive's latest saved copy was read instead, and is marked. From those pages: sentences of the form “a project of…”, “published by…”, “funded by…” (quoted as printed); charity, company and tax registration numbers, linked to the official register where it can be searched by number; the copyright line; what the site declares about itself in its structured data; tracking and advertising account IDs; and, from the domain registry (RDAP), when the domain was registered and by whom, where that is published. Nothing is inferred: a site that names no owner is recorded as naming none.

read: 8,462, not reachable: 1,451. Of these, the pages read gave a domain registration date for 6,886; a tracking or advertising account ID for 5,788; a copyright holder for 5,412; a declared organisation (structured data) for 2,833; a statement of who runs, owns or funds it for 1,809; a registration number for 601; a named registrant for 257.

2001-10-18–

Cited sites that share a tracking or advertising account

In short: Groups of different websites that use the same Google, Facebook or Yandex tracking account, which often means one owner or manager.

Groups of two or more cited websites whose pages carry the same Google Analytics, Google Tag Manager, AdSense, Facebook pixel or Yandex Metrica account ID. The same account means the sites are measured or monetised from one account, which usually means one operator; a shared web agency or a copied template can also cause it. Accounts that belong to a platform rather than a site (such as the host account Google's Site Kit plugin puts on every site that uses it), and any ID found on more than 25 cited sites, are left out as shared services. The account IDs are shown so the match can be checked in each site's page source.

Everything read, as JSON, with the address and fingerprint of each page read and the date.

Cited websites: records kept elsewhere

In short: Facts about cited websites from outside records (old saved copies, address records, security certificates), for sites that are gone or have changed.

Facts about cited websites that do not depend on reading the site as it is today. Saved copies: for sites that could not be read live, the same facts as above were read from the Internet Archive's most recent good copy of the home page (found through its capture index), the archived copies of the cited pages that the citations themselves link to, and the site's about and legal pages as archived; where the Internet Archive had none, from the most recent copy in Common Crawl's public web crawl. DNS: the site's name servers, mail servers, the domains its SPF record allows to send its mail, and site-verification codes (from Google, Facebook, Microsoft and others) published in its DNS. Certificate logs (for sites that could not be read live): the certificates issued for the site, from the public Certificate Transparency logs, with the earliest seen and the other domains named on the same certificate; certificates naming more than 10 domains are left out of that list, because hosting companies issue such certificates for unrelated customers. Citations: the names editors gave the site in the citations, the earliest access date stated, and the earliest saved copy of a cited page.

Of the 1,451 sites that could not be read live: no saved copy found: 744, read from saved copies: 707.

Domains whose current registration began after they were cited

In short: Website addresses registered after the article cited them, which can mean the address now belongs to someone else. The site's title then and now is shown.

The domain registry (RDAP) gives a registration date later than the Internet Archive's copy of a page on that same domain that a citation links to. Both dates are shown, with the copy and the article citing it. Access dates written in citations are not used, because editors who update a link to a site's new domain often keep the old access date. A registration date after the copy means the domain was registered anew after that date; the record does not show whether the holder changed. Some registries report the latest transfer as the registration date.

Accounts that added links to two or more such domains after registration began

Counted from the analysed articles' word histories: the revision that added each link's domain to the text. Only domains whose home page title today shares no word with the title then are counted, so registry dates that only reflect a transfer are left out (a revived site that kept its old name is left out as well). Accounts are shown as one-way IDs that differ from the IDs on the editors page; the diffs are on each article's page under “Links to check”. An editor can add a link to a site that looks like the original in good faith; the table records when, not why.

Cited sites that share a DNS or certificate value

In short: Different cited websites that share the same server records or security certificate, which can mean they are run together.

Groups of two or more cited websites with the same site-verification code in their DNS records; groups whose name servers, mail servers or authorised mail senders are on the domain of another cited site; and pairs of cited websites named together on one certificate. The same verification code means the same account verified the sites with that service, which can be an agency or host acting for several clients. Some cited sites also provide mail or name servers to the public (a webmail or cloud company, for example); their groups are shown like any other. Servers on domains that are not cited sites are recorded per site but not grouped. Values found on more than 25 cited sites are left out as common services.
